name: Social desirability bias
statement: Asked to report their own behaviour, people are said to shade the answer towards what looks respectable, overstating acts like voting and hiding stigmatised ones.
meaning: This is a property of the instrument rather than of the mind behind it. A respondent who has understood the question and remembers the answer can still report something else, because a question about drug use or turnout is also a question about how the respondent wants to be seen. Two different things travel under the one name. The first is the response bias itself, the gap between what a person did and what a person reports. The second is a supposed trait, scored by scales such as the Marlowe-Crowne, on which some people come out higher than others. Paulhus divided the second into impression management, where the respondent consciously dissembles to an audience, and self-deception, where the respondent actually believes the flattering answer. Almost all the usable evidence concerns the first. Acquiescence and the other response styles are a separate literature with its own experiments, and entry 176 covers them.

origin.who: Douglas P. Crowne and David Marlowe
origin.note: Their paper is "A new scale of social desirability independent of psychopathology", and the title states its purpose. The article was read in full from the Internet Archive's scan of the August 1960 issue. Earlier scales took their items from clinical inventories: Allen Edwards drew his 39-item scale from the MMPI validity scales and the Manifest Anxiety Scale. Crowne and Marlowe object that a student who denies fitful sleep may simply be well rather than flattering himself. Their own items come from behaviours "culturally sanctioned and approved but which are improbable of occurrence", on page 350. An item analysis on 76 students cut 47 candidates to the 33 that survive, 18 keyed true and 15 false.

evidence: The evidence that carries weight compares answers with records. Ansolabehere and Hersh matched 26,181 respondents in the 2008 Cooperative Congressional Election Study against commercial voter files across fifty states. Reported turnout was 84.3% and validated turnout 68.5%. Among respondents validated as non-voters, 52.0% said they had voted, against 25.3% in 1988, 27.7% in 1984 and 27.4% in 1980 in the validated National Election Studies. Error in the other direction was almost absent, with 99.1% of validated voters reporting a vote. Experiments agree. Holbrook and Krosnick asked a national telephone sample of 898 American adults about the 2000 presidential election either directly or through an item count list, a design that lets a respondent report a vote without naming it. Direct questioning yielded 72.0% turnout and the item count technique 52.4%, a one-tailed difference at z = 1.66. Three parallel internet surveys showed no such gap. Administration mode moves disclosure the same way. Gnambs and Kaspar pooled 460 effect sizes from 48 samples and found more admission of sensitive behaviour on computer than on paper. The corrected odds ratio was 1.19, with a 95% interval on the log odds ratio of 0.10 to 0.25, and it reached 1.29 for sexual behaviour.

replication.headline: Across 124 samples, shielding the answer raises reported rates of sensitive behaviour by 8.5 percentage points, and yet the correction cannot be relied on in any single study.
replication.detail: Ehler, Wolter and Junkermann pooled 303 estimates from 89 articles that compared the item count technique with direct questioning. The pooled difference was 0.085 in proportions, which the authors give as 8.5 percentage points in the direction of more disclosure, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.065 to 0.105 under robust variance estimation. The result held across three estimators, and tests found no sign of publication bias. Heterogeneity was close to total, with I² above 90%, and the 95% prediction interval ran from -0.112 to 0.281. Direct questioning therefore understates on average, while a researcher planning the next study cannot assume the shielded version will beat it. The technique did better on items people over-claim, such as turnout and green behaviour, than on strongly stigmatised acts, which is the opposite of what the theory predicts.

study.cite: Ehler, I., Wolter, F., & Junkermann, J. (2021). Sensitive questions in surveys: A comprehensive meta-analysis of experimental survey studies on the performance of the item count technique. Public Opinion Quarterly, 85(1), 6-27.

replicated.unit: proportion, item count technique minus direct questioning

limits: Whether records beat self-reports is itself contested. Berent, Krosnick and Lupia report that matching methods badly underestimate how many Americans were registered, which pushes validated turnout down, and that among respondents who can be matched to a record the accuracy of self-reports is high. They call the apparent gain from validation an illusion made of two biases: matching failures that depress registration, and survey respondents voting more often than the people who did not answer. The remedies are also weaker than their reputation. Holbrook and Krosnick found the randomised response technique produced turnout of 111.6% in their telephone study, an impossible figure, and non-response to the randomised items reached 15.8% against 0.6% for the direct question. Coverage is narrow: the record-linked work is almost all American turnout, and the mode meta-analysis draws 343 of its effects from the United States and 300 from substance use. Tourangeau and Yan's review was read only in abstract, so no figure from it appears here; its stated conclusion is that misreporting on sensitive topics is common and largely situational, which is the framing this entry follows.
misreadings: The first error is filing this with the judgement biases. Nothing here says people reason badly; it says a self-report is a social act with a listener, and the same person gives a different answer to a screen than to an interviewer. The second is treating a score on a social desirability scale as a correction factor. Lanz, Thielmann and Gerpott meta-analysed 41 samples and 8,980 participants and found the correlation between such scores and prosocial behaviour in economic games was 0.04, with a 95% interval of 0.01 to 0.07. If the scales measured a bias the correlation should be negative, and if they measured a virtuous trait it should be clearly positive, so the authors advise dropping them. Paulhus had already argued that only impression management should be controlled, since the scales loading on self-deception showed no significant change when responses were made public. The third error is the inference that survey answers are worthless. In the validated sample where half of non-voters claimed a vote, other reports held up. Race matched the record for 94% to 95% of respondents in the southern states that register it, on 4,540 cases, and party registration for 93% to 95% in the states that hold it, on 11,292. Misreporting attaches to the items that carry credit, not to the questionnaire.

Read in full from the Internet Archive's scan of the August 1960 issue; the quotation and the item counts come from pages 349 to 351. An earlier note here called it paywalled and unobtained.

It quotes the 1960 definition with an added "of", and this entry follows the original wording instead.
